item.title: Converting your Italian consultant into an employee
item.description: Your Italian freelancer has become part of the team. Why that is a risk, and how to move them onto an Italian employment contract through an EOR.

item.title: EOR, freelancer or Italian subsidiary: three routes for a Nordic company
item.description: How a Swedish, Danish, Norwegian or Finnish company can have people working in Italy: an Employer of Record, a freelancer, or its own srl. Pros, risks, timing.

item.title: Fixed-term or permanent in Italy? A decision guide for Nordic employers
item.description: Italy, like Sweden, treats the open-ended contract as the norm. When a fixed-term contract fits, when it backfires, and what it means for retention.

item.title: Non-compete clauses in Italy: why a Nordic template will not survive
item.description: Italian non-competes are valid only if written, paid and limited in time, place and activity. What Nordic employers must change in their standard clause.

item.title: Remote work in Italy: the written lavoro agile agreement Nordic companies need
item.description: A remote-first Nordic company cannot rely on a policy page in Italy. Lavoro agile needs a written agreement. What it must cover and how to prepare it.

item.title: Provanställning vs periodo di prova: probation in Italy for Nordic employers
item.description: Swedish and Italian probation both run up to six months. The Italian version has stricter form rules and ends without notice. What to set up before day one.

item.title: LAS vs Italian dismissal rules: what a Swedish employer should expect
item.description: Both Sweden and Italy require a valid reason to dismiss. The grounds, the notice and the procedure differ. A practical comparison for Nordic HR teams.

item.title: Italian CCNL vs Swedish kollektivavtal: same idea, different default
item.description: Swedish managers know collective agreements. The Italian CCNL works on a similar logic, with one big difference: it applies from the first hire.
